questions.q: What does PHP serialize() produce from an in-memory object?
o: A JSON document of the object property names only
A string encoding of the object class and property values
A compressed binary blob that browsers cannot display
A Base64 copy of the object with the class name removed
questions.x: serialize() converts an object into a string that can be stored or sent. That string records the class name, how many properties it has, and each property name and value. unserialize() turns the string back into an object.
questions.h: Serialization is object-to-string. What details must that string keep so PHP can rebuild the object later?

questions.q: In PHP serialized form, what does a leading O mean?
o: Object, with a class name length after it
Output type for printed debug dumps
Optional field that may be omitted later
Ordered array of scalar string values
questions.x: O marks an object. Next comes the class name length, then the class name, then the property count. s marks a string, including property names and string values.
questions.h: PHP uses a one-letter type prefix. What kind of value does uppercase O stand for?

questions.q: Why is unserializing data an attacker can edit dangerous?
o: unserialize() always makes a network call that can be redirected
PHP ignores types, so every property becomes a callable method
The server rebuilds whatever object the attacker put in the string
Serialized strings cannot be stored in cookies without crashing
questions.x: If an application stores serialized objects in cookies and blindly calls unserialize() on them, the attacker can change the string. PHP then reconstructs the object the attacker chose, not the original one.
questions.h: unserialize() rebuilds objects from the string. Who controls that string if it lives in a cookie?

questions.q: In the serialized format, what does the number after the class name mean?
o: The PHP version that wrote the string
How many properties the object contains
The byte length of the entire cookie value
The access level of the first property name
questions.x: After the class name, the format records the property count. For example a User object with username and access_token has 2 properties. Each property then appears as a name and a value.
questions.h: The partial breaks the format into class name, then a count, then properties. What is being counted?

questions.q: Which statement about PHP serialization is correct?
o: serialize() turns objects into strings
unserialize() encrypts those objects
All of these statements are true
O marks a serialized PHP array
questions.x: serialize() converts an in-memory object into a string. unserialize() rebuilds the object, it does not encrypt. A leading O means object, not array. All is wrong because those last two claims are false.
questions.h: Look at the format notes. What does serialize() produce, and what does a leading O stand for?
